abstracts.abstract: Current probabilistic reasoning frameworks in clinical decision support systems exhibit fundamental limitations when handling multi-source medical evidence with conflicting reliability levels. This paper introduces the Evidential Reasoning Transfer Network (ERTN), a novel theoretical paradigm that reimagines knowledge-based medical systems through the lens of transferable evidential weights. Unlike traditional Bayesian approaches that assume static conditional probabilities, ERTN models medical evidence as dynamically adjustable based on source credibility, temporal relevance, and cross-institutional validation status. The framework employs a hierarchical attention mechanism to propagate uncertainty through diagnostic reasoning chains while maintaining logical consistency with established clinical protocols. We formalize the evidential weight transfer process using information-theoretic measures that quantify the cost of opinion divergence among heterogeneous medical knowledge sources. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that ERTN achieves tighter bounds on diagnostic uncertainty compared to Dempster-Shafer evidence theory while preserving computational tractability essential for real-time clinical applications. The paradigm shift from fixed probability distributions to transferable evidential representations enables more robust reasoning under uncertainty in scenarios where medical knowledge evolves rapidly, such as emerging disease patterns or rare condition identification. This work establishes a new theoretical foundation for next-generation clinical decision support systems that can dynamically adapt their evidential reasoning to the reliability landscape of available medical information.

Predictive modeling in intensive care settings faces a fundamental trade-off between model interpretability and predictive accuracy when handling temporal sequences in electronic health records. This paper presents a significant theoretical advancement in representation learning for clinical time-series data through the Hierarchical Temporal Attention Memory Network (HTAMN). While existing approaches treat vital sign sequences as flat temporal sequences, HTAMN introduces a multi-scale temporal abstraction framework that decomposes clinical time-series into physiologically meaningful hierarchical segments corresponding to organ systems and clinical phases. The theoretical contribution lies in the formal derivation of attention mechanisms that are provably aligned with clinically relevant temporal patterns, ensuring that model reasoning can be traced to specific physiological events. We prove that the proposed hierarchical attention achieves optimal sample complexity for learning temporal dependencies spanning multiple timescales compared to conventional attention mechanisms. The framework incorporates domain knowledge through constrained attention weight structures derived from clinical practice guidelines, enabling seamless integration of knowledge-based constraints without degrading predictive performance. Experimental validation on MIMIC-III and eICU datasets demonstrates that HTAMN achieves state-of-the-art performance in predicting clinical deterioration events while providing clinically interpretable reasoning chains that satisfy the transparency requirements essential for deployment in medical AI systems.

Medical image analysis systems have traditionally employed specialized models optimized for single imaging modalities, requiring costly model development for each clinical application. This paper presents MedFusionX, a novel paradigm-shifting system architecture that enables unified multi-modal medical image understanding through a modality-agnostic knowledge distillation framework. The system introduces the Cross-Modal Medical Concept Embedding space, where diagnostic features from different imaging modalities (CT, MRI, X-ray, ultrasound) are projected into a shared semantic representation aligned with clinical ontology. Unlike previous multi-modal approaches that require parallel datasets, MedFusionX employs a teacher-student architecture where a large language model serves as the knowledge bridge, enabling cross-modal transfer learning from text-rich medical reports. The system architecture incorporates a novel Uncertainty-Aware Fusion Module that explicitly models and propagates imaging quality uncertainty through the analysis pipeline, ensuring appropriate confidence calibration across different clinical settings. Implementation demonstrates real-time inference capability suitable for clinical deployment, with the complete pipeline processing multi-modal inputs in under 3 seconds on standard clinical hardware. The paradigm shift lies in treating medical imaging not as modality-specific tasks but as instances of a unified visual understanding problem with domain-specific adaptation layers. MedFusionX establishes a new architectural template for comprehensive medical image analysis that can rapidly adapt to new imaging modalities and clinical applications.

Clinical natural language processing systems for electronic health records face significant challenges when deployed across institutional boundaries due to vocabulary variations, documentation style differences, and evolving medical terminology. This paper presents ClinicalBERT-X, a substantially improved system architecture for institutional-adaptive medical NLP that significantly advances the state of the art in clinical text understanding. The system introduces a Novel Institutional Calibration Module that learns institution-specific documentation patterns and vocabulary usage through lightweight adapter layers while preserving the foundational medical knowledge encoded in large-scale pre-trained language models. Unlike prior domain adaptation approaches requiring extensive labeled data from each institution, ClinicalBERT-X achieves effective institutional adaptation through self-supervised continual pre-training on local EHR corpora with novel uncertainty-based sample selection that prioritizes institutionally distinctive text patterns. The architecture incorporates a Hybrid Entity Resolution Engine that combines rule-based medical ontology mapping with contextual neural embeddings for robust concept normalization across heterogeneous vocabularies including ICD, SNOMED-CT, and local institution-specific codes. Extensive evaluation across five academic medical centers demonstrates that ClinicalBERT-X achieves consistent performance improvements of 12-18% on clinical NLP tasks including medication extraction, adverse event detection, and disease phenotyping. The system design prioritizes computational efficiency suitable for production deployment, achieving inference speeds 2.3 times faster than comparable multi-institutional models while maintaining superior accuracy on out-of-distribution clinical text.
